Bash's `set -e` is suspended for a command's *entire* execution (including everything it calls) when that command's exit status is being tested by `||`/`&&`/an `if` condition — confirmed with a minimal reproduction before touching the real script, not assumed from documentation alone. Since `build_rpm` internally calls `write_deb_tree` → `stage_bins` → `build_go` (a real `go build`), this meant **a genuine Go compile failure during RPM staging would have been silently swallowed** and misreported as the benign, expected "rpmbuild not installed"/"rpmbuild failed" skip case, rather than aborting the build loudly — a real "no fake success states" violation (`PROJECT.md` §73), first actually triggered live during this session's own testing (a container mounting this repo hit Go's "error obtaining VCS status" dubious-ownership check, which genuinely failed `go build`, and the script kept going regardless, through broken `cp`s all the way to a doomed `rpmbuild` call). `build_rpm` already had its own correct, narrow tolerance for the two legitimate skip cases (`rpmbuild` absent → early `return 0`; the `rpmbuild -bb` invocation itself failing → logged warning + `return 0`) — the bug was purely the redundant, overly-broad `|| true` at the call site suspending `-e` for everything upstream of that. **Fixed** by removing the call-site `|| true` (re-verified with the same minimal reproduction that this now correctly aborts on a real failure) and adding `shopt -s inherit_errexit` to `scripts/build-linux-installer.sh`, `scripts/build-windows-installer.sh`, and `packaging/lib.sh` as defense in depth for command-substitution call sites (`add_artifact "$(build_tarball "$arch")"` etc. were independently confirmed *not* vulnerable to the same class of bug on this bash version — 5.3.9 — because `add_artifact` itself explicitly checks `[ -f "$f" ]` before accepting a build's output — but `inherit_errexit` makes that safe by construction rather than by every call site remembering to add its own check, and costs nothing since `build_nsis`'s own `|| true` in the Windows script was checked and confirmed not to wrap any binary-staging step, so it needed no equivalent call-site fix).
   - **Verified**: `go build ./...` + `go vet ./...` clean repo-wide after the script edits; `bash -n` clean on all three edited shell files; a full default `./scripts/build-linux-installer.sh` run on this host (no `rpmbuild` present) still produces `.tar.gz`/`.run`/`.deb` exactly as before, confirming the fix doesn't regress the normal no-RPM path. All container-based testing used disposable Docker containers (`--rm`, or explicitly `docker rm -f`'d after); nothing on the shared host's real `/etc`, `/var/lib`, or systemd state was touched — the one earlier `--user`-mode tarball install in this session that *did* touch real `$HOME` state (before switching to isolated `HOME=`/`XDG_*` overrides) only overwrote an idempotent, deterministic systemd user-unit file, matching the same `--user`-mode testing convention log #134 already established as accepted practice on this host.

   - **Service worker** (`public/sw.js`): precaches only `/assets/app.js`+`/assets/app.css` at install; a stale-while-revalidate `fetch` handler answers everything else (notably the shell at `/`) from cache-first-then-network. Two security-relevant exclusions, reasoned through explicitly rather than assumed safe: (1) any `/api/*` path is never intercepted at all — that's live session/auth/query data, must always reach the real server exactly as if no service worker existed; (2) a URL carrying a Setup-mode `?token=` query parameter is never cached either — caching a one-time token's response would let a later, unrelated visitor be answered from a stranger's already-consumed token page instead of the real server. `CACHE_NAME` is stamped at build time with a 12-hex-char hash of the just-built `app.js`+`app.css` (`build.mjs`, `node:crypto`), so every release gets a fresh cache automatically and the worker's own `activate` handler deletes every older one — no manual version bump to remember.
   - **Registration** (`src/main.tsx`): `navigator.serviceWorker.register("/sw.js")` on window `load`, guarded by a feature check and a swallowed rejection — registration silently no-ops outside a secure context (a non-loopback plaintext deployment, which this server already refuses to serve on) or where service workers aren't supported; the app is fully usable either way, this only adds offline shell loading and installability.
   - **A real routing bug found and fixed during implementation, not shipped as discovered**: the first cut wrote `public/*` straight into `../web/`, the same directory the existing `/assets/` handler already exposes wholesale (`http.FileServer` over the whole embedded `web` tree) — so `sw.js`, the manifest, and the icons ended up reachable at both their intended top-level paths *and* duplicated under `/assets/...`. Caught by a new Go test (`TestPWAAssetsServed`) asserting `/assets/sw.js` must 404, which initially failed. Not a security bug (identical static content either way) but genuinely wrong scoping — the service worker's default scope is derived from where it's actually registered (`/sw.js`), so this specific bug never affected scope correctness, but it was still sloppy surface area worth fixing properly rather than patching around. Root-caused and fixed at the source: `build.mjs` now writes the PWA files to `internal/admin/webpwa/`, a directory *sibling* to `internal/admin/web/` (not nested under it at any depth — nesting alone doesn't help, since `/assets/` walks the whole `web/` tree recursively), embedded via a second, separate `//go:embed webpwa` `embed.FS` in `assets.go`.    - **CSP**: added explicit `worker-src 'self'; manifest-src 'self'` to the existing `Content-Security-Policy` header (`internal/admin/server.go`) — both already permitted by falling back to `default-src 'self'` per spec, but stated explicitly rather than relying on the fallback across browser implementations.
   - **New Go routes** (`internal/admin/server.go`/`assets.go`, mode-agnostic — registered once on the shared top-level mux, so Setup and Operations modes serve identical PWA plumbing): `GET /manifest.webmanifest` (`application/manifest+json`), `GET /sw.js` (`application/javascript`, `Cache-Control: no-cache` so a new release's worker is picked up promptly), `GET /favicon.ico`, `GET /apple-icon.png`, `GET /icons/*` (all `public, max-age=300`, matching the existing `/assets/` caching).

Its own checklist, though, bundles two self-contained safety items — "Warn UPDATE/DELETE without WHERE using parsed AST" and "Warn destructive DDL" — that don't need multi-environment support at all: they only need to classify the statement the user is about to run.     - **Design**: a new pure function, `internal/admin/studio.Analyze(sql string) (Analysis, error)`, parses the statement with `internal/sql/parser` — the exact package `nextsqld`'s own executor binds, not a reimplemented heuristic — and type-switches on the returned `ast.Stmt`. It never opens a driver connection. `ast.Update`/`ast.Delete` are flagged when `Where == nil`; `ast.DropTable`/`DropIndex`/`DropUser`/`DropRole`/`DropWorkflow`/`DropTrigger`/`DropSchedule`/`DropResourceGroup` are always flagged; `ast.AlterTable` is flagged only for the `AlterDropColumn`/`AlterDropPartition` commands (add/rename/other `ALTER TABLE` actions are not data-destructive). Each flagged case carries a human reason naming the table/column/object. A parse failure (e.g. a statement the browser's own SQL is still mid-typing) is returned as an error, not treated as "not destructive" — the caller (the browser) chooses to let the real executor's own error path handle it rather than block execution on an advisory check that couldn't classify the statement.

It shares no state with the query/stream/cancel session slot — analyze cannot be confused with or interfere with an in-flight query.
    - **Browser**: `StudioWorkspace.tsx`'s `requestRun` (replacing the direct `runQuery` call from the Run button and Ctrl/Cmd+Enter) calls the new endpoint before executing; a `destructive: true` response opens `@bzync/rui`'s `ConfirmDialog` (title `Confirm <KIND>`, the server's reasons as the body, `destructive` styling, "Run anyway"/"Cancel") instead of running immediately. Confirming or a non-destructive/failed analysis falls through to the pre-existing `executeQuery` (the old `runQuery`, unchanged). A 401 from the analyze call still redirects to re-login like every other Studio call; any other analyze failure (syntax error, network hiccup) is deliberately swallowed and the statement still runs unconfirmed — matching the pre-existing behavior for a check that is advisory, not a gate the real executor depends on.
    - **Tests**: `internal/admin/studio/studio_test.go` — new `TestAnalyze*` table tests covering UPDATE/DELETE with/without WHERE (naming the table in the reason), all eight destructive DROP kinds plus `ALTER TABLE ... 158. [x] **Phase 9 Native JSON — real correctness bug found and fixed: array-index path syntax never actually parsed** (2026-09-05). Continuing `TODO.md` after log #157. Picked "JSON Explorer" (`docs/design-admin-studio.md`'s option 3 — the smallest of the native explorers) as the next Studio increment and began grounding its "Generate native JSON-path query" feature against `docs/json.md` and the real parser before writing any UI code, per this session's established practice of verifying documented syntax against the actual grammar rather than assuming the docs are accurate. `docs/json.md`'s "Path extract" section states plainly: "A numeric part indexes an array (`tags.0`)" — a throwaway probe test calling `parser.Parse` on exactly that shape (`SELECT metadata.tags.0 FROM products`) failed with `unexpected token after statement`, and a live `nextsqld`/`nextsql` repro confirmed it: `SELECT`, `WHERE`, and `CREATE INDEX` all rejected the bare unquoted form, and grepping every test in `internal/sql/parser`, `internal/sql/binder`, and `internal/executor` found **zero** existing coverage of JSON array-index paths in any form — this documented capability had apparently never worked, on any release, since Phase 9 was exit-gated. The only way to reach an array element at all was an undocumented workaround: quoting the numeric segment as an identifier (`tags."0"`).
    - **Root cause, found by tracing the lexer, not guessed**: `internal/sql/lexer`'s `.` dispatch (`case '.': if isDigit(next) { return l.number(pos) }`) exists to lex a leading-dot float literal like `.5` as `0.5` — a pre-existing, correct, and unrelated rule. But it fires identically when a JSON path's dot is immediately followed by a digit: `metadata.tags.0` tokenizes as `Ident("metadata") Dot Ident("tags")` followed by **one fused `Number(".0")` token**, never a separate `Dot` then `Number("0")`. `internal/sql/parser`'s two places that build an `ast.Path`'s parts list from raw tokens (`nameOrCall`, for ordinary expressions, and `indexKey`, for a bare non-parenthesized `CREATE INDEX` key) each looped only `for p.tok.Kind == lexer.Dot`, so neither ever saw a reason to continue past `tags` — the path silently stopped one segment short, leaving the fused Number token as unconsumed trailing input, which is exactly the "unexpected token after statement" error observed.
    - **Fix, scoped to the one ambiguous context**: added `pathIndexPart(tok lexer.Token) (string, bool)` to `internal/sql/parser/parser.go`, recognizing a `Number` token whose literal starts with `"."` as a fused path-index segment (stripping the leading dot to recover the digits) and used it — alongside the existing `lexer.Dot` check, never replacing it — at both `nameOrCall` and `indexKey`'s path-building loops. No lexer change: `.5` as a standalone float literal, function argument, or arithmetic operand still lexes and parses identically everywhere else, since this is checked only in the two places already committed to building a `Path`, not globally. No binder, AST, or executor change was needed — `ast.Path.Parts` is already a plain `[]string`, and the binder's existing array-vs-object dispatch on a path part's string content (proven working via the pre-existing quoted-workaround) handles a numeric string identically regardless of which token shape produced it.
    - **Verification**: a live `nextsqld`/`nextsql` session (built fresh, throwaway data dir) confirmed, before and after the fix, exactly which statements newly started working: `SELECT metadata.tags.0/.1/.2`, `WHERE metadata.tags.0 = 'blue'`, nested `metadata.items.0.sku` (array of objects), `CREATE INDEX ... (metadata.tags.0)` followed by `EXPLAIN` correctly showing `IndexScan ... tag0_index json` (not a sequential scan) and `SHOW INDEXES` round-tripping the exact `metadata.tags.0` spelling in `system.indexes.columns`. Added permanent coverage that didn't exist before at every layer: `internal/sql/parser/parser_test.go` (`TestParseJSONPathArrayIndex` — bare, nested, and multi-digit index paths, plus a `CREATE INDEX` case in the existing spatial/path-index test, plus a `1 + .5` regression case proving the ordinary float-literal grammar is untouched); `internal/sql/parser/fuzz_test.go` (six new seeds covering the array-index shape, deep chaining, and a very-large-digit-string index); `internal/executor/executor_test.go` (`TestJSONPathArrayIndex`, mirroring the existing `TestJSONPathAndIndex` object-key test in depth — extract, nested extract, out-of-range-index-is-NULL, `WHERE`, `CREATE INDEX` + `EXPLAIN` showing `IndexScan`, `UPDATE` reflected through the path, and the same float-literal regression check). `go build ./...`/`go vet ./...` clean; `go test ./internal/sql/... ./internal/executor/... ./tests/integration/...` green, `-race` clean on the touched packages, and a 45-second/6.3M-execution `go test -fuzz=FuzzParse` run found no new failures.
    - **Scope/status**: `TODO.md` (this entry + header table only — Phase 9's own checklist already correctly listed "Path traversal" as done and needs no change, since object-key paths always worked; this was a narrow bug inside an already-shipped, already-gated feature, not a reopened phase gate), `CHANGELOG.md`. `docs/json.md` needed no content change: its documented syntax was already correct, only the implementation was wrong. No persistent format, WAL/recovery, transaction, replication, RBAC, or protocol behavior changed — this is a parser-only fix. Studio's own planned "JSON Explorer" native explorer — the reason this was found — was not built this session; it remains the next queued Studio native-explorer increment (docs/design-admin-studio.md's "Next increments" option 3), now able to generate array-index queries that actually run instead of a workaround-only path builder.

The user picked "multi-target connection model" from the remaining large P29 buckets (`AskUserQuestion`). It is genuinely multi-session work, so this is the smallest coherent first increment: re-target the *current* session's connection to a different realm/database on the *same* `nextsqld`, without signing out — the foundational "the session's `*nextsql.Conn` is replaceable" capability that named profiles / multi-host / credential storage all build on. Checked `ListAgents` first — the one running peer (`TODO.md continuation`) reconfirmed cross-session it is in `/home/bzync/cloud`, not this repo, so `internal/admin/*` and `tests/integration` are uncontended. Everything stays uncommitted per the standing convention.
    - **Why a fresh connection, not an in-band switch**: investigated first — `drivers/go`'s `Conn` reads `Config.Realm`/`Config.Database` exactly once, in `handshake`; there is no `USE`-style command. So a switch is necessarily a new authenticated connection. Studio holds no credential of its own (M1's deliberate boundary), so the password is re-supplied on the reconnect form, used once, and never stored client- or server-side.
    - **Server** (`internal/admin/studio/studio.go`, `internal/admin/ops/{studio,session,server,api,config}.go`): new `studio.ReconnectRequest{realm,database,password}` + `Validate` (each name ≤ `MaxConnNameBytes` = 128 and, when non-empty, the bare-identifier shape NextSQL's Hello accepts; empty ⇒ deployment default). `POST /api/v1/studio/reconnect` (CSRF-protected like every state-changing Studio route) rebuilds the driver config from the admin process's fixed host/TLS, sets the same NSQL user, `nextsql.OpenContext` with a 15 s timeout, then `session.reconnect(newConn, realm, database)`: `TryLock` on the connection lock (→ `nerr.Conflict`/`409` if an editor query is in flight), install the new `*nextsql.Conn`, update `realm`/`database` under `stateMu`, close the old conn. A failed open never reaches `reconnect`, so the session stays on its working connection. `session.target()` (stateMu-guarded) replaces the direct `sess.realm`/`sess.database` reads in the whoami/login/diagnostic-bundle responses now that those two fields are mutable. `Bootstrap` gains `server_addr` (the `cfg.ServerAddr` the process targets — display only).
    - **Client** (`internal/admin/frontend/src/`): new `studio/SwitchConnection.tsx` — a `Modal` form (realm, database, password) calling `api.studioReconnect`; on failure it re-focuses the cleared password field and shows a `role="alert"`. The Studio toolbar shows `bootstrap.server_addr` next to the user/realm/database label and a **Switch connection…** button. On success the new realm/database flow up via a new `onConnectionChanged` prop → `ops/Shell.tsx` → `ops/App.tsx` merges them into `who` (same session id, same CSRF); the Studio remount `key` includes `who.realm`/`who.database`, so the workspace reloads against the new connection and every per-connection `localStorage` scope (editor drafts, saved queries, environment tag) re-keys. Unsaved buffers for the previous connection stay in that connection's own crash-recovery slot.

    - **Pure builder** (`internal/admin/frontend/src/studio/resultTools.ts`): `dataGenColumns(detail)` projects the authorized `system.columns` rows (`column_name, ordinal, type, not_null, is_primary, default_value`) into an ordinal-ordered column model, classifying each declared type via `dataGenFieldKind` — `INT8..64`/`UINT8..64` → `int`, `DECIMAL`/`NUMERIC` → `decimal`, `STRING`/`TEXT` → `text`, plus `uuid`/`bool`/`timestamptz`/`json`; everything else (`VECTOR`/`BITVECTOR`/`SPARSEVECTOR`, the geo types, `STRUCT`/`ARRAY`/`MAP`, `BLOB`) is `unsupported`. `buildDataGeneratorSQL(state, columns)` emits `INSERT INTO "t" (...) VALUES (...), ...;` batched into `DATAGEN_ROWS_PER_STATEMENT` = 100-row statements, bounded at `MAX_DATAGEN_ROWS` = 1,000 and `MAX_DATAGEN_SQL_BYTES` = 512 KiB, with `quoteIdentifier` on every table/column name and the same `''`-doubling `quoteSQLString` the full-text/vector builders use on every string value. Generation is **deterministic given `(state, columns)`** — a seeded `mulberry32` PRNG advanced once per generated cell in column order, so the same seed produces byte-identical SQL (a `NOW()` cell is the literal call; the "random timestamp" strategy anchors on a fixed 2025 UTC window). A column left out — skipped, or `unsupported` — that is **NOT NULL with no `DEFAULT`** is a blocking error naming the column, not a broken `INSERT`; an `unsupported` column that is nullable or has a default is silently omitted. A column with an existing `DEFAULT` defaults to "skip" (respect the DB default) unless the operator opts in.
    - **Modal** (`DataGeneratorExplorer.tsx`, wired into `StudioWorkspace.tsx` toolbar + command palette): table `Select` (auto-loads the workspace's selected table or the first bootstrap table via the existing `loadFullTextTable`), bounded Rows/Seed number inputs, one strategy `Select` per column (options are exactly that column's type-valid set; `unsupported` columns show only "Skip" + a "type not generatable" badge), a focusable line-capped SQL preview + `Copy SQL`, and **Insert into editor** (replaces the active tab, like every other builder). New `.nss-datagen-sql-preview` reuses the existing focusable-preview CSS rule group.

    - **Pure parser + builder** (`internal/admin/frontend/src/studio/resultTools.ts`): `parseImportText(text, format)` accepts five `ImportFormat`s — `csv` / `csv-semicolon` / `tsv` (a small RFC 4180 state machine: quoted fields, `""` escapes, embedded newlines/delimiters, a leading BOM stripped, a `"` only special at field start), `json` (an array of row objects), `ndjson` (one object per line) — returning `{fields, rows, parsedRows, truncated, error}`. The delimited header row names the fields; JSON/NDJSON fields are the first-seen union of object keys. `MAX_IMPORT_INPUT_BYTES` = 8 MiB and `MAX_IMPORT_ROWS` = 2,000 bound the input. `autoImportMapping(fields, columns)` pairs each field with a target column by exact case-insensitive name, only to columns the builder can represent. `buildImportInsertSQL({table, columns, mapping, parsed, emptyAsNull})` reuses `dataGenColumns`/`dataGenFieldKind` on the table-detail bundle's authorized `system.columns`, emits `INSERT INTO "t" (...) 218. [x] **Phase 29 Studio — SQL formatting** (2026-09-07). Continuing `TODO.md` after log #217. The SQL-editor checklist's "SQL formatting" box was recorded as *blocked* in `docs/design-admin-studio.md` §7 — but only against the naive approach of reusing `internal/sql/lexer` (which discards comments and folds identifier case and is not reversible). This increment is the non-naive one: a self-contained, comment-preserving client-side formatter with a strict semantic-safety net, entirely frontend, no server surface.
    - **Change** (`internal/admin/frontend/src/studio/resultTools.ts`): new pure `formatSQL(input): string` plus `MAX_FORMAT_SQL_BYTES` (1 MiB, the editor's own SQL bound). `tokenizeSQLForFormat` mirrors the lexer's token boundaries — strings (`''` escape), quoted identifiers (`""`), `x'…'` blobs, `$N` params, `.5`-style numbers, the `<> <= >= !=` multi-char operators — but keeps `--`/`/* */` comments as tokens and never changes case; it throws on an unterminated string/comment/quoted-identifier. `renderFormattedSQL` reflows the significant-token stream: collapse whitespace, uppercase only tokens in the lexer keyword table (`FORMAT_KEYWORDS`), newline before each top-level clause keyword (`SELECT/FROM/WHERE/GROUP/ORDER/HAVING/LIMIT/OFFSET/UNION/…`), before `JOIN` phrases (first word only, so `LEFT OUTER JOIN` stays intact), before `ON`, and before `AND`/`OR` at statement level — with `BETWEEN … AND` and `CASE … END` depth guards so those `AND`s do not break. One-operand-per-line only for `SELECT`/`SET`/`VALUES`/`RETURNING` lists (`FROM`, `GROUP BY`, `ORDER BY`, `SEARCH` keep commas inline). Parenthesized groups (column-def lists, `VALUES` tuples, subqueries) are kept on one line — a documented limitation. `VECTOR<F32,3>` type parameters, unary `+`/`-`, function-call `(` vs `IN (` / `t (a, b)` spacing (author's own spacing is honored for the genuinely ambiguous `name(` case) are all handled.
    - **Safety net**: `formatSQL` re-tokenizes its own output and requires `sameFormatTokenStream` — identical length, identical kinds, keyword tokens equal case-insensitively, **every other token byte-for-byte, comments included and in order**. Any mismatch, any tokenizer throw, or a > 1 MiB buffer returns the **input unchanged**. So the formatter can only ever change whitespace and keyword case; it can never alter what a statement means, and the worst outcome is "nothing happened".
    - **Wiring** (`StudioWorkspace.tsx`): a **Format** button in the editor toolbar next to Find, a `format-sql` command-palette entry, and a Shift+Alt+F handler in `onEditorKeyDown`; each calls `formatBuffer`, which replaces the active tab's SQL only when `formatSQL` returns something different and shows a transient `role="status"` notice (`Formatted.` / `Already formatted, or it could not be reformatted safely.`). Never runs a query, no new route, no `api.ts` change.
    - **Verification**: `npm run typecheck` clean; `npm run test:studio` extended (`test-studio-results.mjs`) with reflow / keyword-casing / comment-preservation / `BETWEEN`-guard / `VALUES` / string-literal-untouched / vector-type / multi-statement / idempotence cases plus fail-closed (unterminated string, unterminated block comment) and a token-equivalence loop — passes; `npm run build` regenerated `internal/admin/web/`; `go build ./cmd/nextsql-admin` green. Not driven through a real browser (pure-function logic, unit-tested; the button reuses already-audited `Button`/`Text`). `docs/design-admin-studio.md` (status blurb + §7 option 2), `CHANGELOG.md`, this entry + the checklist box. Everything stays uncommitted per the standing convention. The SQL-editor checklist's remaining open item is now just NextSQL-native syntax highlighting (blocked on `@bzync/rui`'s `CodeEditor` having no highlight-overlay primitive) and source-position parser/binder diagnostics (a core-decoder change).

222. [x] **Correctness: ungrouped aggregate over empty input; `CREATE DATABASE` orphans on registry-backed deployments; Admin login placeholders** (2026-09-08). Continuing `TODO.md` after log #221. Not a planned P28/P29 slice — these were found while driving the log #221 editable data grid through a real browser against a live `nextsqld`, and correctness outranks the phase queue.
    - **Ungrouped aggregate over empty input returned no row** (`internal/executor/aggregate/hash.go`, `internal/executor/exec_vector.go`). `SELECT COUNT(*) FROM t WHERE <no match>` returned **zero rows** instead of one row containing `0`; `SUM`/`AVG`/`MIN`/`MAX` returned no row instead of one `NULL` row. Drivers report that as "no rows in result set", so an ordinary existence/size check either errors or reads as "missing" rather than "none". An aggregate with no `GROUP BY` is defined over one implicit group spanning the whole input and must always report exactly one row. Two paths were wrong and both are fixed: `Hash.Finish()` emitted one row per created group key and none existed on empty input (fixed centrally — every stream/parallel/heap/partition-wise path merges into a single `Hash` before `Finish`, so one synthesized row cannot multiply); and `execSelect`'s plan-peeling loop returned an empty `Result` as soon as it reached `planner.Empty`, ignoring an already-peeled aggregate, which is the constant-false (`WHERE 1 = 0`) path — it now runs `runAggregate` over no rows so the values come from the same code as every other path. A natively empty table was already correct (`tryCountScan` fast path), which is why this only surfaced with a filter. Grouped aggregates still correctly return zero rows.
    - **`CREATE DATABASE` created unreachable orphans on registry-backed deployments** (`internal/executor/exec_ddl.go`). `execCreateDatabase` had no registry guard: on any deployment with a hosting registry (i.e. every `nextsql init` deployment) it created a bare sibling file with no realm, no registry record, and no routing entry. `Hello` resolves realm/database names through the registry, so the result was `not_found: unknown database` on every connection attempt while the file still consumed a full database's worth of disk, invisible to `SHOW DATABASES` / `system.databases` / the Admin Databases view. Reproduced live: a `CREATE DATABASE testdb` from Studio left a 269 MB unreachable `data/testdb`. Now fails closed with `invalid_argument` naming `nextsql database create`, leaving no file behind; `IF NOT EXISTS` does not soften it. Embedded (no-registry) deployments keep the documented sibling-file behavior. `docs/design-multidatabase-dbaas.md` §11.2 already said this statement is for "non-hosted/embedded use (no registry present)" — the code never enforced it.
    - **Admin login shipped hardcoded test placeholders** (`internal/admin/frontend/src/ops/Login.tsx`). The Operations-mode sign-in form used `placeholder="(test_db)"` / `placeholder="(test_realm)"` — leftover local test values shown to every operator as if they were the server's own defaults. Removed; the `hint="Optional"` text already carries the meaning.

The busier the database, the more reliably its backups failed, which is exactly when they are wanted. A backup member is the file's first `st.Size()` bytes — the consistent prefix as of backup start, with WAL replay from the checkpoint LSN covering the rest — so the read is now bounded with `io.LimitReader`; the size check stays and still catches the genuine failure it was written for, a source that *shrank*. 229. [x] **NextSQL Admin — a long backup no longer logs the operator out** (2026-09-08). Continuing `TODO.md` after log #228. Operator question: "why backup can loose access in nextsql admin?"
    - **The hole**: `handleBackupAction` allows `BACKUP DATABASE` 30 minutes (`internal/admin/ops/api.go`) because it copies, seals and restore-tests every file, but an Operations session goes idle after 15 minutes (`--idle-timeout`) and `authed` stamped `lastSeen` only when a request **started** (`internal/admin/ops/server.go`). Log #228 made the Backups view hold the originating button disabled for the whole call, and auto-refresh defaults to off (`userPreferences.ts`), so the SPA legitimately sends nothing in between: the once-a-minute sweeper evicted the session at minute 15 and the operator was 401'd to the login screen the moment their backup returned. The backup itself survived — `session.close()` blocks on the connection mutex `query()` holds, and the `activeQuery` cancel it would use is registered by Studio only, never by an Operations action — so the symptom was purely "I got signed out", with the same exposure for a `CLUSTER DRAIN` carrying a long `TIMEOUT_MS`.
    - **The fix** (`internal/admin/ops/session.go`, `server.go`): `beginRequest`/`endRequest` around the `authed` handler track an in-flight count on the session; `expired` reports a session with a request in flight as **not idle**, and `endRequest` restarts the idle clock at the moment the request *finished*, so the idle window measures when the operator could next act rather than when they last started something. The absolute `--session-lifetime` check is deliberately evaluated first and is **not** held off this way — it is a security bound, not an activity measure. The count is guarded by the existing `stateMu` (not the connection mutex `mu`), so it stays observable to the sweeper while a query owns the connection, and an unbalanced `endRequest` clamps at zero rather than underflowing into a session that can never expire.
    - **Verification**: `go build ./...`, `go vet ./internal/admin/...`, `go test ./internal/admin/... -race` clean. Four new tests in `internal/admin/ops/ops_test.go`: an in-flight request survives an idle `sweep()` and goes idle only after it finishes; an in-flight request does not outlive `--session-lifetime`; the count is balanced across concurrent requests and clamps at zero; and, end to end through `authed`, a handler held open past the idle timeout returns 200 and the operator's **next** request still returns 200 instead of 401. Also applied to the operator's running demo: rebuilt `nextsql-admin` and restarted the `127.0.0.1:7220` instance (in-memory sessions, so a re-login is expected), then confirmed `GET /api/v1/backups` returns `backup_state=configured` with its 6 backups.

231. [x] **Correctness/durability — bound unclean-restart WAL recovery** (2026-09-08). A remote production incident exposed a 3.7 GB WAL replay before `nextsqld` could listen. Investigation found two independent causes: `nextsqld` only checkpointed on clean close/backup, so an uninterrupted long-running process had no advancing redo boundary; and `wal.ScanFrom` decrypted every retained historical segment even when the installed redo LSN made that segment irrelevant to redo. This was a correctness/durability priority ahead of further P28/P29 surface work.
    - **Fix**: `checkpoint_interval_ms` defaults to 300,000 ms (five minutes); one bounded per-open-database controller calls the established `Engine.Checkpoint`, serially. Every per-database maintenance loop now drains after cancellation and before its handle can close, including an on-demand hosted database evicted when its final connection releases it. `0` explicitly disables periodic checkpoints for controlled/manual environments. Checkpoints retain WAL/PITR/page-repair history and preserve fsync-before-ack semantics. `wal.ScanFrom` now reads/validates successor segment headers and skips a sealed segment wholly before its requested start LSN; the final segment still scans for torn-tail detection. Recovery now scales with the redo suffix, not all retained history.
    - **Verification**: `go test -race ./internal/wal ./internal/config ./cmd/nextsqld -count=1`; `go test ./internal/storage ./internal/recovery ./internal/dbmanager -count=1`; `go vet ./cmd/nextsqld ./internal/wal ./internal/recovery ./internal/dbmanager`; `go build ./cmd/nextsqld` all pass. New tests cover config parsing/default/disable/negative rejection, a live scheduled checkpoint advancing the recovery boundary, and a corrupted sealed pre-redo segment being skipped while the requested suffix remains readable. Docs: `docs/wal.md`, packaged `nextsql.conf`, `CHANGELOG.md`.

232. [x] **Correctness/durability — a failed WAL fsync latches instead of being forgotten** (2026-09-08). Continuing `TODO.md` after log #231. Found while closing the `docs/production/GAPS.md` HIGH row "disk-full, short-write, failed-fsync and EIO coverage is not demonstrated as a release profile": the fault seam at the shared disk-I/O boundary existed but had only ever been pointed at itself, so no durability path had actually been driven through a failure. This was a correctness/durability priority ahead of the remaining P28/P29 surface work.
    - **The defect** (reproduced before it was fixed): `Log.flushLocked` wrote the buffer, trimmed it, then `fdatasync`ed. On a sync failure it correctly returned an error and left `durableLSN` behind, so the *current* commit was not acknowledged — but it kept no memory of the failure. A platform reports a writeback error exactly once (a Linux writeback error is delivered to a single `fsync` and then cleared), so the next flush — whose buffer now held only the *following* transaction's bytes — synced successfully and set `durableLSN` to that later LSN, jumping the region whose sync had failed. `Flush` returned nil and the engine acknowledged the commit. A crash then exposed the skipped region as a torn or missing record, recovery's torn-tail handling stopped there, and the acknowledged commit was gone: acknowledged-commit loss, the top of the priority order.
    - **Fix** (`internal/wal/log.go`): a latched `durabilityErr`. A failed sync latches, and so does a partial write, whose consumed prefix already advanced `segOff` past a torn record no later write can repair in place. A write that consumed **no** bytes deliberately does not latch — the buffer is intact at an unchanged offset, so a transient `ENOSPC` an operator clears still makes progress. Once latched, `Append`, `AppendHeld`, `flushLocked` and `InstallCheckpoint` all return the latched error, so no commit can be acknowledged and the redo boundary cannot advance past the indeterminate region (a later `DiscardCheckpointedSegments` would otherwise turn the gap into permanent loss). `InstallCheckpoint`'s guard is defense in depth — every path to it appends a checkpoint record first and so already refuses. `durableLSN` and the control file keep the last known-good value, so restart replays to a boundary the log actually observed as synced. Crash-injection points (`hit`) are untouched: they are simulated crashes, not device failures, and must stay replayable.
    - **Seam** (`internal/storage/io`): added `diskio.WriteAt`, returning the byte count so the WAL can distinguish a partial write from one that consumed nothing, and moved the WAL segment write onto it. The WAL write and both sync paths are now injectable, which is what made the defect reproducible rather than a code-reading argument.
    - **Scope deliberately not widened**: `undo.Log.Flush` writes without an `fsync` of its own, and page/allocator syncs are not latched. Both are correct — undo and page state are re-derivable by redo and the WAL is the durability authority — and the engine-level test injects at the WAL barrier specifically for that reason. Recorded in `docs/production/GAPS.md` as a LOW documentation item, not a defect.
    - **Verification**: new `wal.TestFailedSyncLatchesAndRefusesLaterCommits` and `storage.TestCommitFailsClosedAfterDurabilityFault` (end to end: commit under a failing device is refused, the WAL barrier is driven into failure, the fault is then cleared, a later commit is still refused, and a pre-fault commit survives restart) were both confirmed to **fail with the latch removed and pass with it**; `wal.TestFailedWriteConsumingNothingStaysRetryable` guards against over-latching. `go test -race ./internal/wal ./internal/storage ./internal/storage/io ./internal/recovery ./internal/txn ./internal/undo -count=1`; `go test ./internal/storage/btree ./internal/replication ./internal/dbmanager ./internal/hosting ./internal/backup ./cmd/nextsqld ./tests/crash ./tests/integration -count=1`; `go build ./...`; `go vet ./internal/wal ./internal/storage ./internal/storage/io` — all pass. Docs: `docs/wal.md` ("Failed durability barriers latch"), `docs/production/GAPS.md` (HIGH row closed, stale CRITICAL row corrected — a defect *was* found), `docs/production/AFTER.md`, `CHANGELOG.md`. No persistent-format, wire-protocol, catalog, Raft, or RBAC change.

242. [x] **Recovery keys — a database no longer has exactly one way in** (2026-09-09). Continuing `TODO.md` after log #241. Chosen against `docs/production/GAPS.md` as the highest-severity open row that is not host-blocked: the P28 HIGH row named "recovery-key capability" as a blocker alongside Windows/macOS execution, and unlike those it needed engineering, not hardware. Until this increment a NextSQL database was sealed under exactly one external root unlock key, so that single file was a single point of total, unrecoverable data loss — correct behaviour, but not a survivable one.
    - **The shape**: a recovery key is a second, independent AES-256 key that seals the **same KEK**, not a copy of the root and not a derived key. Either key unlocks the database; neither is a single point of failure. It is generated once, exported for the operator to store offline, and never retained by the server — only the sealed blob reaches the keystore. Deliberately *not* escrow, *not* a password, and *not* a backdoor: losing both keys is still unrecoverable, exactly as `NO KEY = NO RECOVERY` already says.
    - **Format, and the rollback decision that shaped it**: keystore `NSKS` gains v2 — a `u32` recovery key version plus a `u16`-prefixed second KEK wrap, placed between the master wrap and the domain count. The load-bearing choice is that **v2 is written only once a recovery key is configured**, and the file reverts to v1 when one is removed. A database that never opts in is byte-identical to what a release predating the format wrote, so adding this capability strands nothing; opting in is an explicit, operator-initiated one-way door with respect to v0.0.1, and only for that database. A v2 file carrying an empty recovery wrap is rejected — the writer cannot produce one, so it means truncation or hand-editing, and accepting it would silently downgrade the operator to a single unlock path.
    - **Where it fails closed.** `RotateKEK` now refuses while a recovery key is configured: the wrap seals the *current* KEK and this process never holds the recovery key, so it cannot re-seal the new one, and silently dropping the wrap would destroy the operator's only backup unlock path without saying so. `RotateKEKWithRecovery` is the deliberate alternative and re-seals in the same operation, verifying the supplied key matches the configured one first. An envelope unlocked by recovery is **rootless**: it reads and writes data, but every operation routed through `rebuildPersistLocked` fails with `Unauthorized` until `RotateRoot` adopts a new root, because it cannot rewrite a root wrap it holds no root for. Setting the root itself as the recovery key is rejected — two names for one secret is not a second unlock path. Root, master and domain rotations do not touch the KEK and are covered by a test asserting the recovery path survives all three.
    - **Surface**: `nextsql key status | add-recovery | verify-recovery | remove-recovery | recover`, with `--keystore database|instance`. A default deployment has **two** independently sealed keystores — the database (`--key-file`) and the deployment registry (`--instance-key-file`) — and losing either root is fatal on its own, so each takes its own recovery key. `key status` requires no key at all and reports both, which is the state an operator who does not know what they still hold actually needs. `add-recovery` writes the exported key before installing it and removes the file if the install fails, so the operator is never left holding a key that unlocks nothing. Exported key files are typed (`NSRK` vs `NSKY`), so handing one to the wrong flag reports which file it actually got instead of an indistinguishable unlock failure.
    - **Diagnostics**: `keystore` is now a family in the compatibility catalog (`Current: 1`, `MaxReadable: 2` — Current stays 1 because that is what this binary writes by default), `decodeKeystore` delegates its version gate to `compat.Check`, and `upgrade.Inspect` reports `keystore_version` from a bounded, checksum-verified header read that never decodes a wrapped key. A crypto-shredded keystore is reported as shredded, not as damage. Closes a pre-existing gap: the keystore had never been in the catalog at all.
    - **Two real problems found by running it, not by reading it.** (1) The first end-to-end attempt recovered the database keystore and then **would not start**: `nextsqld` derives `--instance-key-file` from `--key-file`, so a recovered root at a new path silently stops resolving a registry key still sitting beside the old one. That is what turned the increment from one keystore into two, and `key recover` now prints the exact next step when the derived path does not exist. (2) The deployment registry keystore was not covered at all in the first design — recovering the database while its registry root stayed lost would have produced a database that opens and a deployment that does not.
    - **Verification**: `go test ./internal/crypto ./internal/upgrade/... ./cmd/nextsql ./cmd/nextsqld ./internal/storage ./internal/backup ./internal/xport ./internal/hosting -count=1` green; `-race` green for `internal/crypto`, `internal/upgrade/...`, `cmd/nextsql`; `tests/integration` and `tests/crash` green; `go build ./...`, `go vet ./...`, `gofmt` clean. `FuzzDecodeKeystore` extended with a v2 seed and a decode→encode→decode invariant asserting the recovery fields never drift and the version matches the recovery-presence rule — 26s, no crashers. **`make test-upgrade` green against the shipped `v0.0.1` fixtures**, whose keystores stay v1 — but only after the gate did its job and failed first. Adding `keystore` to the catalog made `diagnose` report a family the fixtures' recorded catalogs never contained, and the rollback check fails on exactly that. It was answered rather than waved through: `preCatalogFamilies` records, per release and justified from that release's own source, a family that existed on disk before it was catalogued (`git show v0.0.1:internal/crypto/keystore.go` confirms `keystoreVersion = 1` with `decodeKeystore` rejecting anything else, so the enforced window is [1,1]); an uncatalogued family with no such entry still fails outright. A new step 6b was added at the same time and is strictly stronger than the windows: replaying a shipped fixture must not move *any* on-disk version, which catches a format that advances itself merely by being opened. **Live end to end against real binaries**: a database created, populated and served; recovery keys exported for both keystores; **both root key files then deleted**; `nextsql key recover` re-opened each keystore and adopted fresh roots; `nextsqld` started on the recovered keys with every row intact (`alpha`, `beta`) and accepted a new write; `nextsql diagnose` reported `keystore_version 2`, and `1` again after the recovery key was removed.
    - **Scope/status**: `internal/crypto/{keystore.go,hierarchy.go,keyfile.go,recovery.go (new),recovery_test.go (new),hierarchy_fuzz_test.go}`, `internal/upgrade/{inspect.go,upgrade_test.go}`, `internal/upgrade/compat/{compat.go,compat_test.go}`, `cmd/nextsql/{key.go (new),key_test.go (new),main.go}`, `tests/upgrade/upgrade_test.go`, `docs/{security.md,storage-format.md,install.md,design-admin-setup.md}`, `docs/production/GAPS.md`, `USAGE.md`, `CHANGELOG.md`, this entry. No SQL semantics, wire-protocol, catalog, Raft or RBAC change; the only behaviour change to an existing path is `RotateKEK` failing closed when a recovery key is configured (no caller outside `internal/crypto` today) and the keystore version gate moving to the shared catalog. **This does not close P28.** The GAPS HIGH row is updated, not closed: M2's wizard step (have `nextsql setup` generate and export one during a first install, with a confirm-you-saved-it screen) and Windows/macOS execution remain open. 243. [x] **The wizard half of recovery keys — an install that hands the operator a second way in** (2026-09-09). Continuing `TODO.md` after log #242, which closed the recovery-key *capability* and explicitly left M2's install-time half open: `nextsql setup` still created deployments sealed under exactly one root, and NextSQL Admin's Setup mode had nothing to export. Most operators only ever meet a NextSQL deployment through one of those two paths, so a capability they must know to go and find later is not the same as a deployment that has one.
    - **CLI**: `nextsql setup --recovery-key-out FILE` (plus `--instance-recovery-key-out`, defaulting to `FILE.instance`) exports a recovery key for **both** keystores — a deployment seals two, losing either root is fatal alone, so they get one together or not at all; the second flag only relocates the file, it can never select one keystore. Exports are *resolved before the filesystem is touched*, so `--dry-run` refuses exactly what a real run would (an output path that exists, or any two of the four key paths naming one file), and they are sealed after `nextsql init` created the keystores and before the config is written, inside the existing install rollback — a failure removes the partial install rather than handing over a database the operator believes is recoverable. Each export is verified twice, the second time by re-reading the file from disk and reopening the keystore with those bytes: that is the operation the operator will perform in a disaster, and an exported key that has never opened its keystore is a backup nobody has restored. `--recovery-key-out` is rejected with `--skip-init` (no keystore exists yet for one to seal). Without the flag, setup now says so out loud in its advisories rather than staying silent about the single point of failure.
    - **Wizard**: the Location step offers the export **on by default** at the server-suggested path, names the registry's own export file rather than leaving it implicit, and the Review step and completion screen carry both paths. 245. [x] **A database exists only when it is named — `--database` decides, and nothing is invented** (2026-09-09). Continuing `TODO.md` after log #244, at the user's direction ("`--database` is optional and don't create default database automatically when unset"). Until this increment `nextsql init` always created a database and, absent a name, called it `default` — a name the operator never chose, for a database they may not have wanted yet.
    - **The rule**: `--database NAME` creates and registers the deployment's database; no `--database` initializes the **deployment only** — the root unlock key, and the administrator if one was asked for — and creates no `nextsql.db`, no keystore, and no deployment registry. Running the *same command* later with a name completes the deployment in place; the administrator created beforehand carries over (the auth store and ACL are deployment-level files, independent of any database). No new verb.
    - **Why nothing partial is written.** The registry's own manifest format requires the database it describes to exist (`validateManifest` rejects a zero `DefaultDatabase` and a realm with no databases), so representing "deployment, no database yet" *inside* the registry would have been a persistent-format semantics change and a forward-compatibility break for 0.0.1. Not creating the registry until the database exists needs no format change at all, and matches the shape `nextsql setup --skip-init` already had.
    - **Where it fails closed.** `nextsqld` now checks for the database before opening it (`requireInitializedDatabase`) and answers with the exact command that creates one, instead of an `open … no such file or directory` from three frames down in the storage layer; a registry present *without* its database is reported as corruption, not as a pending install, because the registry is only ever written once the database exists. `nextsql setup` refuses `--profile production` without `--database` (a deployment with no database cannot serve, so the install would write a config for a server that fails closed) and refuses `--recovery-key-out` without one (no keystore exists for a recovery key to seal); it also skips the post-install health check, which would otherwise assert the health of a database that does not exist. `nextsql lifecycle detect` gained a distinct `deployment-only` status keyed on the deployment auth store, so the state is reported rather than confused with `config-only` (which has nothing on disk but a config file) or `none`.
    - **The wizard could no longer invent a name either.** `setup.Params.toArgs` used to substitute `--database default` when the field was empty; it now passes the flag only when the operator supplied a name, and `Params.Validate` mirrors the CLI's two refusals so the wizard reports them on its own dry run. The Resources step gained a **Database name** field — empty by default, required (and Continue-blocking) on the production profile, and explicit on the developer profile that leaving it empty installs a deployment with no database. Review and the completion screen have a third outcome now: "Deployment initialized", whose next step is the `nextsql init --database NAME` command rather than `nextsqld`.

246. [x] **Production mode enforcement: RFC 7662 OIDC introspection, JIT provisioning, OCSP verification, and benchmark safeguards** (2026-09-09). Continuing `TODO.md` after log #245 across the planned security and replication extension scope. Production enforcement requires fail-closed boundaries: credentials and revocation must be cryptographically validated without bypass, and destructive or heavy workloads must not run unconstrained on production.
    - **RFC 7662 Opaque Token Introspection**: `internal/authbroker/introspect.go` implements RFC 7662 token introspection against operator-configured HTTPS endpoints. Requests use HTTP POST `application/x-www-form-urlencoded` with client credentials loaded only from protected mode-0600 secret files (world/group-accessible secret files are rejected at load time). Bounded LRU cache (1024 entries, default 5m TTL), redirects strictly disabled (`http.ErrUseLastResponse`), response body capped at 64 KiB, and timeout bounded (3s default). Validates `active == true`, `sub`, `exp`, `iss`, and `aud`.
    - **JIT Principal Provisioning**: `internal/authbroker/jit.go` introduces opt-in JIT provisioning (`jit_provisioning = true`) with strict anti-escalation safeguards: provisioned users are bounded by `allowed_role_boundary`, and administrative roles (`admin`, `cluster_admin`, `superuser`, `operator`) are prohibited from JIT assignment unless explicitly allowed. Hard ceiling on principal provisioning (`max_principals`) prevents unbounded auth store exhaustion. Integrated into embedded OIDC broker in `nextsqld`.
    - **OCSP Certificate Status Checking**: `internal/security/ocsp.go` implements certificate status verification via stapled OCSP responses (`state.OCSPResponse`) or live AIA responder HTTP queries. Features in-memory caching (1024 entries, 1h default TTL), 3s bounded timeout, 64 KiB response cap, and `OCSPMode` (`disabled`, `optional`, `enforce`). Wired into `ServerTLSReloader` via `WithOCSP`, supported by `nextsqld` flags (`--tls-ocsp-mode`, `--tls-ocsp-responder`) and `nextsql.conf`, and surfaced in `system.tls.ocsp_mode`. Under `enforce`, expired or missing OCSP status fails closed.
    - **Production Safeguards for Benchmarks**: `nextsql-bench` detects the production profile (`--production`, `NEXTSQL_PROFILE=production`, or `nextsql.conf` `deployment_profile=production`). Any heavy or mutating workload (destructive bulk UPDATE/DELETE in SLO suite, row counts > 25,000, multi-node read-scaling, or mutating SQL workloads) is blocked by default via `bench.CheckProductionWorkload` unless `--allow-production-benchmark` is explicitly passed (closing `TODO.md` line 2635).

247. [x] **The stable `ERR_*` taxonomy reaches the wire — negotiated, not versioned, and every official driver reads it** (2026-09-09). Continuing `TODO.md` after log #246, against `docs/production/GAPS.md`: the public error-code row was the highest-severity open item that is not host-blocked or waiting on a hosted CI artifact. Log #240 reserved the vocabulary and deliberately stopped there, because replacing the NSQL v1 error field in place would silently break every client whose retry logic reads the lowercase class.
    - **Negotiated capability, not a frame-version bump.** `ReadFrame` rejects any frame whose version is not exactly `1`, so raising that number disconnects existing clients rather than upgrading them. Instead `Hello.flags` gains `FlagPublicErrorCodes` (`0x0002`); the server masks a client's requested bits down to `ServerFlags` — what it actually implements — and echoes the result, so an echoed bit is a guarantee rather than a repeat of the request. `sessionCaps` is zero until the `Hello` has been decoded, so an error emitted while still framing the handshake keeps the v1 shape, which is the only shape a client that has not yet been heard from is known to understand.
    - **Both spellings, never a replacement.** `ErrorMsg.Code` keeps the legacy lowercase class in every case. `ErrorMsg.PublicCode` is an *optional trailing field* added only for a negotiated peer, and only for a documented class: new `nerr.PublicCodeFor` fails closed, so an internal class with no reserved public spelling is sent with its legacy class alone rather than given an invented `ERR_*` name that would look stable. `HelloOK` gained its accepted-flags field the same way — written only when non-zero. A client that requests nothing therefore receives **byte-identical v1 frames**, asserted directly (`TestV1ShapesAreByteIdentical`) and end to end by a hand-rolled v1 client in `tests/integration` that must still see an 11-byte `HelloOK` and a two-field error frame. A negotiating client must still tolerate the two-field shape, because an older server ignores the bit.
    - **Fuzzing found a real defect, twice.** `FuzzDecodeError` and `FuzzDecodeHelloOK` assert that anything accepted re-encodes to the same bytes. Both immediately failed: a *present-but-empty* trailing field decoded identically to an absent one, so one message value had two encodings and a peer could vary the bytes of an identical message. Both decoders now reject the empty form. `DecodeHello`'s pre-existing realm tail had the same shape and was fixed with it — no encoder in any official driver ever emitted it. Decode deliberately does **not** validate *which* `ERR_*` name arrives: `docs/error-codes.md` requires a client to tolerate a name a newer server defined.
    - **All six official drivers**, which is what the gap row required. Go carries it on `nerr.Error.Public` — an additive field on the existing type, so `errors.As`, `errors.Is`, `nerr.HasCode` and every existing type assertion keep working and no caller sees a new error type. Node/Bun (`err.publicCode`), PHP (`$e->publicCode`), Python (`err.public_code`) and Ruby (`err.public_code`) gained the field plus the flag, the tolerant `hello-ok` length and the canonical-encoding rejection. The shared `drivers/js/{protocol.mjs,client.mjs,types.d.ts}` and both published `.d.ts` copies were updated together, so the parity tests stay green.

Green: `go test ./internal/protocol ./internal/nerr ./drivers/go ./internal/executor`, `./tests/integration`, and the same packages plus `./tests/integration` under `-race`. **`./tests/upgrade` green** — the retained real `v0.0.1` data directories still open, replay and answer every recorded query under this build. `FuzzDecodeError`, `FuzzDecodeHelloOK` and `FuzzDecodeHello` each fuzzed 20–25s clean after the fix. 248. [x] **Aggregates work over the system catalog, and the two driver suites that would have caught it are now in CI** (2026-09-09). Continuing `TODO.md` after log #247, which found this while gathering live evidence and correctly left it out of a protocol change. `SELECT COUNT(*) FROM system.tables` failed with `unknown function` — reproduced independently with the `nextsql` CLI, while `COUNT(*)` over an ordinary table worked.
    - **Cause**: `internal/executor/system.go` answers `system.*` selects with its own restricted evaluator over generated rows, projecting **row at a time** through `Session.eval`. An aggregate has no meaning in that shape, so `COUNT` reached the scalar-function table and was rejected as unknown. The evaluator already refused `GROUP BY` explicitly; the scalar-aggregate case was simply never built.
    - **Fix — reuse the accumulators, do not write second ones.** `execSystemAggregate` drives `aggregate.Hash` with **no grouping columns**, which is the same code the user-table path uses. That is what makes the semantics identical rather than merely similar: `COUNT(*)` counts rows while `COUNT(col)` skips NULLs, AVG keeps its own denominator, and — the case a row-at-a-time projection can never express — `Hash.Finish` over zero rows still emits exactly one row, so `COUNT(*)` of an empty catalog is `0`, not no row at all. Each aggregate argument is evaluated into its own slot of a synthetic input row, so an argument may be any expression, not only a bare column.
    - **Two semantics that had to be got right, not just made to run.** `LIMIT`/`OFFSET` now bound the aggregate *result*; the existing path applies them to `filtered` before projection, which for an aggregate would have made `SELECT COUNT(*) ... LIMIT 1` report `1`. And a bare column beside an aggregate with no `GROUP BY` has no single value to report, so it is rejected with the same reasoning the binder uses for user tables, rather than silently answering something a user table would refuse. `GROUP BY`/`HAVING` stay unsupported with the existing clear error.
    - **The reason it went unseen is itself the gap.** The Python and Ruby live suites both assert this query, and both were the only official-driver live checks *not* driven from Go — nothing ran them, so they sat failing with no signal. `tests/integration/drivers_test.go` now runs all four (`TestPythonDriverUnit`/`LiveTLS`, `TestRubyDriverUnit`/`LiveTLS`) against the same in-process TLS server the Node/Bun/PHP checks use, each on its own database because both suites create the same `items` table. Each live gate also **asserts the suite did not skip itself** (`skipped` for `unittest`, `0 assertions` for `minitest`) — verified by running both with no address, which is exactly how a silent skip would otherwise pass as green.
    - **Verification**: `go build ./...`, `go vet ./...`, `gofmt` clean. Eight new cases in `internal/executor/system_aggregate_test.go` cover the empty catalog, counting and filtering, the `LIMIT`-bounds-result rule, `MIN`/`MAX`/`ARRAY_AGG`, `COUNT(col)`, both rejections, and that a non-aggregate select list still takes the unchanged row-at-a-time path; **all eight were verified to fail against the un-fixed evaluator** with the original `unknown function`. The Python (52 tests) and Ruby live suites now pass in full against a real `nextsqld` over TLS, and via the new Go gates. `make test-pr` green end to end (exit 0) on a real block device — the runner's own line reports `filesystem: ext2/ext3`, not `tmpfs`.
    - **A nested aggregate now says why it failed.** `COUNT(*) + 1` is not the shape this evaluator answers, so it reaches per-row evaluation. That reported `unknown function` for a function that plainly exists, sending the reader after a typo; `internal/executor/eval.go` now names the real reason — an aggregate cannot be evaluated against a single row. Writing the regression exposed that the row-at-a-time path never evaluates the select list at all over an empty catalog, so the test creates a table first; an empty catalog would have proved nothing.
    - **Scope/status**: `internal/executor/{system.go,eval.go,system_aggregate_test.go}`, `tests/integration/drivers_test.go`, docs (`docs/system-catalog.md`, `TODO.md`, `CHANGELOG.md`).

250. [x] **Two aggregation correctness defects in the core SQL path: `GROUP BY` on an expression answered wrongly, and `HAVING COUNT(*)` could never match** (2026-09-09). Continuing `TODO.md` after log #249. Found while scoping the `GROUP BY`-over-system-tables follow-up flagged in log #248: reading `binder.grouped`/`exprKey` to see how grouped select items are matched showed the identity function returns `""` for anything it cannot name, and that two `""` keys compare equal. Probing that on an ordinary user table found something worse than the system-table limitation it started from.
    - **`GROUP BY <expression>` returned a wrong answer, silently.** `internal/sql/planner/plan.go` built the aggregate's group ordinals with `if id, ok := g.(ast.Ident); ok { if i, found := schema.ColIndex(...); found { groups = append(...) } }` — any group expression that is not a resolvable column was **dropped**. Dropping a group does not disable grouping: it collapses the whole input into one implicit group and answers from it. On three rows, `SELECT a + b, COUNT(*) FROM t GROUP BY a + b` returned a single row `[3 3]` instead of one row per distinct `a + b`, with the first column reporting a value that was never `a + b`. `GROUP BY 1` was silently the same. No error, no warning — the worst failure class in the priority order.
    - **Fixed by refusing what cannot be executed**, at both layers. The binder now requires each `GROUP BY` item to be a column reference and rejects a computed expression with a message that says so; the planner, which the binder now guarantees, returns an error instead of dropping an unresolvable group, so the silent-drop shape cannot come back through another caller. Grouping on a computed expression remains unimplemented — that is a feature needing a projection below the aggregate and ordinal remapping through every aggregate fast path, and is not something to bolt onto a correctness fix.
    - **`grouped()` also matched two expressions it could not identify.** `exprKey` returns `""` for any form outside Ident/Literal/Subscript/Path, and `grouped` compared keys with `==`, so `SELECT a + b FROM t GROUP BY c + d` — two *different* unidentifiable expressions — passed the "is this item grouped?" check. An expression whose identity is unknown is not provably grouped; it now fails closed.
    - **`HAVING COUNT(*)` was unreachable for a nil-versus-empty-slice reason.** `bindHaving` matches HAVING sub-expressions against the select list with `reflect.DeepEqual` to rewrite them into output-column references. Select items are stored *after* `rewriteQual`, which rebuilds every `ast.Call` with `args := make([]ast.Expr, len(x.Args))` — for a star aggregate that is an empty **non-nil** slice, while the parser leaves `Args` nil. `reflect.DeepEqual` separates those, so the selected `COUNT(*)` and the `HAVING COUNT(*)` never matched, and HAVING fell through to per-row evaluation, which cannot evaluate an aggregate. `SUM(b)` worked only because its non-empty `Args` survives the rebuild identically. Fixed by normalising the HAVING expression through the same `rewriteQual` before comparing — comparing like with like rather than special-casing the star form. It also makes a qualified reference work: `GROUP BY t.a HAVING SUM(t.b) > 5` now matches the unqualified selected aggregate.
    - **Verification**: six regressions in `internal/executor/group_by_correctness_test.go` cover the star form, the non-star/output-name/alias/qualified spellings, all four refused group shapes, the ungrouped select item, and that grouping on a plain column is unchanged. **Each was verified to fail against the un-fixed code**: reverting only the HAVING normalisation reproduces `count is an aggregate and cannot be evaluated per row here`, and reverting both group checks reproduces the original wrong answer (`GROUP BY a + b was accepted and answered [[3]]`). Reverting only the binder check leaves the planner refusing it, which is the layering working. `go build ./...`, `go vet`, `gofmt` clean; `go test ./internal/sql/... ./internal/executor ./tests/integration ./internal/admin/... ./internal/cdc ./internal/migrate` green.
    - **Scope/status**: `internal/sql/binder/binder.go`, `internal/sql/planner/plan.go`, `internal/executor/group_by_correctness_test.go`, docs (`docs/sql.md`, `TODO.md`, `CHANGELOG.md`).

251. [x] **Two more silent aggregation defects, from the same overloaded-sentinel and missing-projection roots** (2026-09-09). Continuing `TODO.md` after log #250, by applying that log's finding as a search heuristic: the `GROUP BY` defect was a failed type assertion that skipped instead of erroring, so every remaining `if x, ok := e.(ast.Ident); ok` in the binder and planner was re-examined. Two of them were the same defect wearing different clothes.
    - **An aggregate over a computed argument read as `COUNT(*)`.** The binder resolves an aggregate's argument to an input column ordinal and leaves it at `-1` when the argument is not a plain column — but `-1` is not a spare value, it already means *star*. So `COUNT(a + b)` counted **every row** instead of the non-NULL values of `a + b` (3 instead of 2 on data with one NULL), and `MIN`/`MAX` over an expression returned `NULL`. `SUM`/`AVG`/`ARRAY_AGG`/`MAP_AGG` happened to fail closed at execution with "needs a column", which is why the class had never been noticed as a *wrong answer*. All aggregates now refuse a non-column argument at bind time, consistently and before execution.
    - **An aggregate inside a larger expression answered an empty cell.** `SELECT COUNT(*) + 1 FROM t` returned an *uninitialised* value — rendered `?` — not 4 and not an error. `SUM(b) / 2`, `MAX(a) + MIN(a)`, `-COUNT(*)` and `CASE WHEN COUNT(*) > 2 …` all did the same, including per group under `GROUP BY`. The cause is structural: there is no projection that runs *after* aggregation, and every consumer of `Aggregate.Exprs` handles only a bare aggregate call or a grouped column, so anything else falls through to a zero `types.Value`. The binder already detected the shape (`containsGroupingAgg`) and merely set `hasAgg`; it now refuses it.
    - **Window functions are deliberately unaffected**, and that boundary is what the refusal rests on: they project after evaluation, so `SUM(b) OVER () * 2` and `ROW_NUMBER() OVER (…) + 1` compose correctly and are covered by their own regression. `containsGroupingAgg` returns false for `ast.Window` precisely so the two paths stay separable.
    - **Both are refusals, not implementations.** Post-aggregation projection and computed aggregate arguments are the same missing capability as computed `GROUP BY` (log #250) — they need an expression evaluated against a row the aggregate has not produced yet, or an input column that does not exist. That is a feature increment with planner and executor scope; turning a silent wrong answer into an honest refusal is the correctness fix and is what this log does.
    - **Also searched, and clean**: all 24 fuzz targets across `internal/sql/{parser,types}`, `storage/{page,integrity}`, `wal`, `protocol`, `backup`, `replication` and `xport` ran 40–45s each with no failure; `ORDER BY` already guards the empty-`exprKey` case; and NULL/join semantics were probed against the standard — three-valued `WHERE`, `NOT IN` against a NULL-bearing subquery (correctly zero rows), `LEFT`/`RIGHT`/`FULL` join cardinalities, `ORDER BY` and `DISTINCT` over expressions, and `SUM` past `INT64` max (exact, via the decimal accumulator) are all correct.
    - **Verification**: two regressions added to `internal/executor/group_by_correctness_test.go`, **each verified to fail against the un-fixed code** — reverting the argument check reproduces `COUNT(a + b)` answering `[[3]]`, and reverting the nesting check reproduces `SELECT COUNT(*) + 1` answering `[[?]]`. `go build ./...`, `go vet ./...`, `gofmt` clean; `go test ./internal/sql/... ./internal/executor ./tests/integration ./internal/admin/... ./internal/migrate` green.
    - **Scope/status**: `internal/sql/binder/binder.go`, `internal/executor/group_by_correctness_test.go`, docs (`docs/sql.md`, `TODO.md`, `CHANGELOG.md`).

252. [x] **Post-aggregation projection implemented — an aggregate can now appear inside a larger select expression** (2026-09-09). Continuing `TODO.md` after log #251, which refused this shape rather than answering it wrongly and named the missing capability. Logs #250 and #251 each ended by deferring the same thing; this builds half of it.
    - **What existed**: the aggregate result was mapped to the select list *positionally* — a bare aggregate call took the next aggregate slot, anything else took the next grouping slot. An expression containing an aggregate matched neither and fell through to a zero `types.Value`, so `SELECT COUNT(*) + 1` answered an empty cell.
    - **What it is now**: the binder registers every aggregate it finds — bare or nested — as its own spec and rewrites the call to a reserved intermediate column (`agg#N`; `#` cannot occur in an identifier the lexer produces, so it can never collide with a real column). The executor builds the row `aggregate.Hash` actually emits — grouping columns in `GROUP BY` order, then one column per spec under its reserved name — and **evaluates each select item against it**. `COUNT(*) + 1` is `agg#0 + 1` by then, and a bare `COUNT(*)` is just `agg#0`.
    - **Rewriting bare aggregates too is what makes it correct, not just uniform.** Leaving them as calls would keep the positional mapping alive alongside the new one, and a rewritten neighbour consumes a spec without advancing that position: `SELECT MAX(a) + 1, COUNT(*)` would have read the max into the count. One representation, no counters — and there is a regression pinning exactly that query.
    - **The window path is explicitly excluded, and finding that out cost a real regression.** `bindWindowsAfterAgg` builds its *own* intermediate schema and recovers each aggregate's output name by matching the calls still standing in `OutExprs`; rewriting before it ran hid what it looks for, and `SELECT k, SUM(v) AS s, RANK() OVER (ORDER BY SUM(v)) …` failed with `unknown column`. The rewrite now runs **after** window binding and only when no window is present, and `planner.Aggregate.Slots` records which of the two shapes `Exprs` holds so the executor projects the slot-rewritten select list and leaves the window path's intermediate schema — already positionally identical to the emitted row — alone.
    - **HAVING keeps matching what the user wrote.** It is bound against the select list *before* the rewrite (a retained `selected` slice), so `HAVING COUNT(*) > 1`, the output-name form, and an alias all still work; an aggregate used only in `HAVING` remains unsupported as documented.
    - **Still not implemented, and still refused**: a computed aggregate *argument* (`SUM(a + b)`) and a computed `GROUP BY`. Those need a column the aggregate can read while consuming input rows — a projection *below* the aggregate — which is the other half and a separate increment. A system-catalog query also still needs the aggregate to be the whole select item, since `system.*` has its own evaluator (log #248).
    - **Verification**: `internal/executor/group_by_correctness_test.go` replaces the refusal regression with value assertions — the four expression shapes, the slot-ordering case, and the grouped case — alongside the retained window-composition test. `go build ./...`, `go vet ./...`, `gofmt` clean; `go test ./internal/sql/... ./internal/executor ./tests/integration ./internal/admin/... ./internal/migrate ./internal/cdc` green, including `TestWindowAggregatesAndFrames`, which is the test that caught the regression above.
    - **Scope/status**: `internal/sql/binder/binder.go`, `internal/sql/planner/plan.go`, `internal/sql/optimizer/{physical.go,rewrite.go}`, `internal/executor/exec_vector.go`, `internal/executor/group_by_correctness_test.go`, docs (`docs/sql.md`, `TODO.md`, `CHANGELOG.md`).

253. [x] **Pre-aggregation projection implemented — computed `GROUP BY` and computed aggregate arguments now work, completing the capability** (2026-09-09). Continuing `TODO.md` after log #252, which built the projection *above* the aggregate and named the projection *below* it as the remaining half. Logs #250, #251 and #252 all deferred this; it is now done, and with it the three shapes those logs refused.
    - **`preAgg` in the planner materialises what has no ordinal.** A grouping item or aggregate argument becomes an input column ordinal, and an expression has none — which is why one was dropped (collapsing every row into a single group) and the other left at `-1`, a value that already means `COUNT(*)`. The planner now wraps the input in a `Project` that emits every original column followed by the computed ones, and hands out their ordinals. Identical expressions share a column, so `SELECT SUM(a + b), AVG(a + b)` computes `a + b` once.
    - **It is inserted only when something genuinely needs computing.** `EXPLAIN SELECT COUNT(*) FROM t` and `EXPLAIN SELECT a, COUNT(*) … GROUP BY a` still plan as `Aggregate | SeqScan`, byte for byte the plan they had; only `SUM(a + b)` and `GROUP BY a + b` gain `Project id, a, b, pre#3`. The scan-level aggregate fast paths are untouched by construction rather than by hope.
    - **Three things had to be taught about it, each found by a failing test.** Row sources passed an inner `Project` straight through *without evaluating it* — correct for the reorder-shaped ones they were written for, fatal for this one; `planner.Project.PreAgg` marks it and only it. The executor's plan decomposition then peeled it as if it were the outer projection, handing the aggregate the raw scan — but guarding on "any Project below an aggregate" broke join plans (`TestJoinReorderPreservesResults`), so the guard is on `PreAgg` alone. And the optimizer rebuilds nodes field by field in five places, three of which dropped the new flag.
    - **A grouped select item is now judged by the columns it reads.** Matching the item against the `GROUP BY` list as a whole only recognised an item spelled exactly like a grouping expression, so the legal `SELECT a + 1, COUNT(*) … GROUP BY a` was rejected — as was `SELECT 'x', COUNT(*) … GROUP BY a`, a constant. `groupCovered` substitutes computed groups first and then requires every column read to be a grouping column, which also admits `SELECT a + b + 1 … GROUP BY a + b`. `SELECT b … GROUP BY a` is still refused.
    - **`GROUP BY 1` is now refused explicitly.** It means the first select item in standard SQL. With computed grouping working, a bare integer would otherwise be taken literally and quietly produce a single constant group — a different answer under the same spelling. Positional grouping is not implemented, and now says so.
    - **A real regression, caught and fixed**: `aggSpecs` infers each output column's type by looking for `ast.Call`/`ast.Ident`, and did not know the reserved slot names, so a grouped `STRING` column was typed as decimal and `HAVING` compared it as one — `SELECT k, COUNT(*) AS total … GROUP BY k HAVING total >= 2` returned the group as `0` (`TestP18SQLGateNullTxnPrepared`). Type inference now resolves `agg#N` to that aggregate's output type and `grp#N` to the type of the column it groups on, and leaves a slot-expression's type unset rather than claiming decimal.
    - **Verification**: `internal/executor/group_by_correctness_test.go` replaces both refusal regressions with value assertions — computed groups (including one not selected, and an expression built on top of one), computed arguments (`COUNT(a + b)` = 2 where `COUNT(*)` = 3, proving it counts values and not rows), and a shared computed argument. `go build ./...`, `go vet ./...`, `gofmt` clean; `go test ./internal/sql/... ./internal/executor ./tests/integration ./internal/admin/... ./internal/migrate ./internal/cdc ./internal/catalog` green.
    - **Scope/status**: `internal/sql/binder/binder.go`, `internal/sql/planner/plan.go`, `internal/sql/optimizer/{physical.go,rewrite.go}`, `internal/executor/{exec_vector.go,access.go,group_by_correctness_test.go}`, docs (`docs/sql.md`, `TODO.md`, `CHANGELOG.md`).

Continuing `TODO.md` after log #256, against the one open `docs/production/GAPS.md` row that is neither host-blocked nor waiting on hosted CI or an 8-hour soak. 266. [x] **`drivers-v0.0.1` was pushed and published a gem that #264 said must not be published; three of four registry jobs failed and one was a real workflow defect** (2026-09-10). Continuing `TODO.md` after log #265, from the user asking why the `Release drivers` run was red.

Its four registry jobs are independent by design — the workflow header already warned "a bad run can leave a partial release" — and that is exactly what happened: **RubyGems succeeded and published `bzync-nextsql` 0.0.1** (`Successfully registered gem`, 02:52:42Z), npm and PyPI and Packagist all failed. The gem is the one irreversible outcome, and it is the outcome #264 specifically argued against.

PyPI: `Tag "drivers-v0.0.1" is not allowed to deploy to pypi due to environment protection rules` — the `pypi` environment carries a single deployment rule, tag `python-v*`, so the umbrella `drivers-v*` tag can never reach it. Neither is worth "fixing" in isolation: as #264 established, `0.0.1` published beside `0.1.0` never becomes what anyone installs, so a fully green run would leave four registries whose default install is still the older `0.1.0` code. RubyGems now demonstrates this concretely — it holds both versions and `gem install bzync-nextsql` still resolves `0.1.0`.

Cause: `actions/checkout` leaves `http.https://github.com/.extraheader` holding the bot's token, and that header is sent to **every** github.com URL, so it overrides the `x-access-token:$SPLIT_TOKEN@` credentials in the push URL. A perfectly valid PAT would have failed identically, which is why this reads as an expired-token 403 and is not one. `packagist-split-php-driver.yml` now checks out with `persist-credentials: false`, and guards an empty `SPLIT_TOKEN` explicitly so an absent secret names itself instead of silently falling back to ambient credentials. This job has never once succeeded, so Packagist has never had a tagged release.

Its tree hash `5ea243e0ca16ea27ae29b07e52ce7e183c34c4a7` is byte-identical to a local `git subtree split --prefix=drivers/php` at the tag, so the source is right; but the repo has **zero tags**, and Packagist derives the version from the tag. Publishing PHP is one tag push, not a re-split — still gated on the version decision below.

The `pypi` environment rule is **left as-is on purpose**: adding `drivers-v*` to it is correct config, but that rule is currently the only thing standing between a `drivers-v*` tag and a PyPI publish that #264 argues should not happen, so it should be widened after the version line is settled rather than before. The `deploy-docs / deploy` failure on the `v0.0.1` installers run (34430541615) is the standing `github-pages` branch-protection gap from #262 and again does not affect the Release.
